card.name: Ramanattam
card.tagline: The 17th-century Keralite dance drama born from royal rivalry to portray the Ramayana.
card.profile: Ramanattam is a traditional dance drama form native to Kerala, India, created under the patronage of King Veera Kerala Varma (Kottarakkara Thampuran) between 1653 and 1694 AD. Formulated as an answer to the Sanskrit dance drama Krishnattam, Ramanattam presents the complete story of the epic Ramayana written in the local Manipravalam style. The drama spans eight distinct daily performances, covering the narrative arc from Rama's incarnation to his ultimate crowning at Ayodhya. Serving as the direct precursor to Kathakali, it laid the foundations for theatrical presentation, costuming, facial acting, and musical accompaniment in Keralite dance performance.
card.insight: In 1657 AD, after being told his court lacked the sophistication to appreciate Krishnattam, Kottarakkara Thampuran composed Ramanattam across eight nightly plays.

card.profile_long:
Ramanattam stands as a landmark performance art in the cultural history of Kerala, India, originating in the mid-17th century under the visionary patronage of Veera Kerala Varma (1653–1694 AD), also known as the Kottarakkara Thampuran. The genesis of this classical temple art was born out of artistic and political rivalry. Following the creation and rise of Krishnattam by King Manavedan, the Zamorin Raja of Calicut, in 1657 AD, its fame expanded rapidly across Kerala. When the Raja of Kottarakkara requested the loan of the Zamorin's Krishnattam troupe to perform at a royal palace wedding, the Zamorin refused and insulted the ruler, declaring that the Kottarakkara court possessed neither the artistic taste nor the intellect to appreciate the complex Sanskrit form.

Deeply offended by this slight, Kottarakkara Thampuran resolved to create a parallel tradition of dance drama based on the epic Ramayana. Unlike the Zamorin's Krishnattam, which was composed in classical Sanskrit—the language of the gods—Thampuran authored the text of Ramanattam in Manipravalam, a rich blend of Malayalam and Sanskrit that made the high epic accessible to his local court and subjects. He authored the narrative in eight comprehensive daily installments: Puthrakameshti, Seetha Swayamvaram, Vicchinnabhishekam, Kharavadham, Balivadham, Thoranayudham, Sethubandhanam, and Yudham. Each poetic section was written to be enacted over the course of a single day, taking the audience on a complete journey from the sacred incarnation of Rama through the Rama-Ravana War and Ravana's defeat, culminating in Rama's triumphant coronation at Ayodhya.

Ramanattam is widely acknowledged as the immediate stem and structural blueprint for the world-renowned dance drama Kathakali. Later, the King of Kottayam (Kottayath Thampuran) integrated elements of Ramanattam and Krishnattam, expanding the narrative repertoire using themes from the epic Mahabharatha to form Kathakali at the Mridangashaileshwari temple in Muzhakkunn. Because Kathakali directly evolved from Ramanattam, the performance style, visual aesthetic, costuming, facial expressions, bodily acting, and traditional background music of the two art forms are deeply interconnected, preserving 17th-century performance dynamics within South Indian classical tradition.

sections.origins_and_history: Ramanattam was created in Kerala, India, under the patronage of Veera Kerala Varma (AD 1653–1694), known as Kottarakkara Thampuran. Its creation was catalyzed by an insult from King Manavedan, the Zamorin of Kozhikode, who in 1657 AD refused to send his Krishnattam troupe to perform at a wedding in Kottarakkara, stating the court would not understand it. Spurred by political and artistic rivalry, Kottarakkara Thampuran composed an eight-part dance drama based on the epic Ramayana in the Manipravalam literary style. Ramanattam became the immediate stem for Kathakali, which was later developed by Kottayath Thampuran at the Mridangashaileshwari temple in Muzhakkunn.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance drama is structured to be performed in eight sections, with each section enacted over a single day. The performance incorporates expressive acting, facial expressions, and movement tailored to tell the dramatic narrative of the Ramayana. The structural presentation and acting style directly inspired Kathakali. Detailed physical footwork, hand gestures, meter, and step counts are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: Ramanattam features background vocal and instrumental accompaniment designed to support the dramatic presentation of the epic text. The vocal text is composed in Manipravalam across eight daily poetic segments. Specific drum types, scales, and instrumental ensembles are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Ramanattam originated as a temple art and royal court performance in Kerala. Its visual costuming and presentation style served as the direct aesthetic basis for Kathakali. Precise garment materials, headwear, and facial paint recipes are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ramanattam is a sacred temple art presenting the narrative of the epic Ramayana. Its eight daily plays depict key spiritual and dramatic chapters: Puthrakameshti, Seetha Swayamvaram, Vicchinnabhishekam, Kharavadham, Balivadham, Thoranayudham, Sethubandhanam, and Yudham, ending with Rama's crowning at Ayodhya.
sections.notable_figures: Key historic figures associated with Ramanattam include Veera Kerala Varma (Kottarakkara Thampuran, AD 1653–1694), who authored the plays and founded the art form; King Manavedan (Zamorin of Kozhikode), whose refusal to share Krishnattam sparked its creation; and Kottayath Thampuran, who later adapted Ramanattam into Kathakali.
sections.regional_variants: Ramanattam originated in Kottarakkara in southern Kerala and heavily influenced the development of Kathakali at the Mridangashaileshwari temple in Muzhakkunn, northern Kerala.
sections.lineage: Derived as a direct response to Krishnattam (created by Zamorin Raja of Calicut in 1657 AD), Ramanattam served as the foundational parent tradition that evolved into Kathakali under the development of Kottayath Thampuran.

claims.text: Ramanattam was created under the patronage of Veera Kerala Varma (AD 1653–1694) alias Kottarakkara Thampuran.
Ramanattam is based on the Ramayana and is divided into eight poetic sections to be enacted in eight days.
The eight sections cover the story from Rama's incarnation to his crowning at Ayodhya.
Ramanattam was composed in Manipravalam style while Krishnattam was written in Sanskrit.
Ramanattam is widely believed to be the immediate stem of Kathakali.
Kathakali and Ramanattam share strong similarities in presentation, costuming, acting, and music.

episode_brief.logline: Discover how a 17th-century king transformed a bitter court rejection into Ramanattam, the eight-day sacred dance drama that birthed Kathakali.
beats: The 1657 dispute: Zamorin of Calicut insults Kottarakkara Thampuran, refusing his request for a Krishnattam troupe.
Kottarakkara Thampuran composes the Ramayana in eight nightly parts using the popular Manipravalam script.
The staging of the epic battles: Rama-Ravana War enacted through expressive mime and music.
